(CNN) — Two former presidents reflected Monday on their greatest regrets in office, each revisiting issues that continue to trouble the nation years later.

Former presidents and political rivals Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush, who now share philanthropic efforts, appeared together at a question-and-answer forum before the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana.

Asked about his greatest regret after leaving office, Bush said he now wonders whether he should have tried to force Saddam Hussein from power at the end of the first Gulf War in 1991.

“I’ve thought a lot about it,” he told the gathering. “But at the end of Desert Storm, the question was whether we should have kept going down that road of death and slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up, laid his sword on the table, and surrendered. And the common wisdom was that he wouldn’t do that.”

But Bush said a conversation with an FBI agent who interrogated Saddam after his capture has caused him to reconsider.

Recalling their exchange, Bush said: “I said, ‘What if we just said he had to come to surrender—would he have done it?’ And this guy said, ‘I’m absolutely convinced he would have.’ My experts tell me he wouldn’t have.”

Bush said, “We ended it the way we said we would,” describing the operation as a military success, but he noted that a cleaner conclusion “would have been perfect.”

“If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table,” he added, “I think it might have avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him.”

On a day when President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the latest U.S. envoy, Clinton discussed his failure to achieve peace between Israelis and Palestinians.

“My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency, which the Israelis accepted,” Clinton said.

“If he had done that ... we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel when not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over the West Bank then than they do today,” Clinton said.

“And if he had taken that deal, we would have had a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think, normal, peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors.”

Clinton said such an agreement would have strengthened the United States’ ability to address other regional challenges.

“We’d be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one,” he said. “And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that.”

Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to “stop the Rwandan genocide” and not succeeding in passing a new health care plan.

He said “presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made” with historians because doing so teaches important lessons. Clinton said he discussed such challenges during a lunch with Obama and the four living presidents, adding, “You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones.”

“All of us know,” Clinton said, “if you make enough decisions, you’re going to make a few that aren’t right.”

(CNN) — On Monday, two former U.S. presidents spoke about the decisions they most wish had gone differently during their time in the White House, pointing to problems that still affect the country years afterward.

Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush, once political opponents, have since worked together on charitable initiatives. The two former presidents appeared jointly at a question-and-answer event hosted by the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana.

When Bush was asked what he regretted most after leaving office, he said he has since questioned whether he should have made a stronger effort to force Saddam Hussein from power at the close of the first Gulf War in 1991.

Speaking to the audience, Bush said he had often considered the issue. At the end of Operation Desert Storm, he explained, the question was whether U.S.-led forces should have continued moving forward, despite the likelihood of more death and bloodshed, until Saddam appeared and formally surrendered by laying down his sword. At the time, Bush said, the prevailing judgment was that Saddam would never agree to such a surrender.

However, Bush said a later discussion with an FBI agent who questioned Saddam after his capture caused him to rethink that view. Bush recalled asking the agent whether Saddam would have surrendered if the United States had simply demanded that he come forward and do so. According to Bush, the agent replied that he was “absolutely convinced” Saddam would have complied, although Bush’s own advisers had told him the opposite.

Bush said the war ended as the United States had promised it would, and he described it as a military victory. Still, he said a more definitive conclusion would have been ideal. He added that if the United States had attempted to compel Saddam Hussein to personally surrender and symbolically lay his sword on the table, some of the later problems caused by Saddam might have been avoided.

On the same day that President Barack Obama sent George Mitchell to the Middle East as the newest American envoy, Clinton spoke about his own disappointment over failing to secure peace between Israelis and Palestinians.

Clinton said his greatest regret was that he could not convince Yasser Arafat to accept the peace proposal Clinton presented near the end of his presidency, a plan the Israelis had accepted.

Had Arafat agreed, Clinton said, the region would have built on seven years of movement toward peace. He noted that in 1998, there was one year — the only one in Israel’s history, he said — in which no one was killed in a terrorist attack. Clinton also said Palestinians then had greater authority over the West Bank than they have now.

If Arafat had taken the offer, Clinton said, there would have been a Palestinian state, and he believed Israel and all of its Arab neighbors would by now have normal, peaceful relations.

Clinton argued that such an agreement would also have strengthened the United States’ position on other Middle Eastern challenges. He said the U.S. would have been in a better place to address Iran and that granting the Palestinians a state while building a constructive, cooperative interdependence in the Middle East would have removed roughly half of the arguments used by terrorists worldwide. He said achieving that outcome would have saved more lives, helped more people, and done great good, and he wished he had been able to make it happen.

Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to halt the genocide in Rwanda and not succeeding in passing a new health care plan.

He added that presidents should be open with historians about the mistakes they made because those experiences offer lessons. Clinton said he had discussed such difficulties during a lunch with Obama and the four living presidents, explaining that the goal is for each new president to make new mistakes rather than repeat old ones.

Clinton also observed that anyone who makes many decisions will inevitably make some that turn out to be wrong.

**NEW ORLEANS** — Former Presidents Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush offered a rare moment of public reflection at a National Automobile Dealers Association forum, speaking candidly about the decisions from their presidencies that still weigh on them.

Appearing together in New Orleans, the two former presidents — once political rivals and later partners in humanitarian work — were asked to name their biggest regrets from office.

Clinton pointed to the United States’ failure to act more forcefully during the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, where hundreds of thousands of people were killed in a matter of months.

“I think I could have done more,” Clinton said in substance, describing the crisis as one of the most painful chapters of his presidency. Clinton has previously said that stronger international intervention might have saved significant numbers of lives.

Bush, the nation’s 41st president, cited his broken “no new taxes” pledge, a defining controversy of his administration. During his 1988 campaign, Bush famously told voters, “Read my lips: no new taxes.” But amid budget pressures, he later agreed to a deficit-reduction deal that included tax increases — a move that angered conservatives and followed him into his unsuccessful 1992 reelection campaign against Clinton.

At the New Orleans event, Bush acknowledged the political cost of the decision while framing it as an effort to address the country’s fiscal problems.

The conversation highlighted the unusual relationship between the two men. Clinton defeated Bush in the 1992 presidential election, but the pair later developed a warm friendship, working together on disaster relief efforts after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and Hurricane Katrina.

Their appearance before the auto dealers’ group mixed policy discussion, personal reflection and humor, with both former presidents drawing on their years in office to address leadership, decision-making and the burdens of the presidency.

The forum came as the auto industry and its dealers were grappling with economic uncertainty, giving the former presidents a platform to discuss not only their own administrations but also broader questions about government, business and public responsibility.

Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton offered sharply personal reflections on foreign policy, war and presidential decision-making, discussing Saddam Hussein, the Gulf War, Middle East peace efforts, Rwanda and the burden of mistakes made in the White House.

Bush, whose presidency was defined in large part by the 1991 Gulf War, defended the decision to use force after Saddam Hussein’s Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990. He described Saddam as a brutal and dangerous leader whose aggression could not be allowed to stand, emphasizing that the U.S.-led coalition’s goal was limited: expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait and restore that country’s sovereignty.

Bush also reiterated a position he held after the war — that the coalition should not have pushed on to Baghdad to remove Saddam from power. He argued that doing so would have fractured the international coalition, exceeded the United Nations mandate and drawn the United States into an open-ended occupation of Iraq. That decision remained one of the most debated aspects of his presidency, particularly after the later 2003 Iraq War under his son, President George W. Bush.

Clinton, who succeeded Bush in 1993, reflected on the challenges of dealing with Saddam during the 1990s, including weapons inspections, sanctions and periodic U.S. military strikes. Clinton said Saddam remained a persistent threat to regional stability, though his administration sought to contain Iraq rather than launch a full-scale war to topple the regime.

The two former presidents also discussed Middle East peace, an issue both pursued while in office. Bush pointed to the 1991 Madrid Peace Conference, which helped bring Israelis and Arab states into direct negotiations after the Gulf War. Clinton reflected on the Oslo peace process and the 2000 Camp David summit, where he tried unsuccessfully to broker a final agreement between Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat.

Clinton expressed frustration that a comprehensive peace agreement remained out of reach, saying the failure to close a deal was one of the great disappointments of his presidency. Bush likewise stressed that American presidents can help create diplomatic openings, but lasting peace ultimately depends on decisions made by regional leaders.

On Rwanda, Clinton spoke with particular regret. His administration has long been criticized for failing to intervene during the 1994 genocide, in which an estimated 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi civilians, were slaughtered over roughly 100 days. Clinton acknowledged that the United States and the international community did not act quickly or decisively enough, calling Rwanda one of the clearest failures of his time in office.

The former presidents also addressed the broader question of presidential mistakes. Both suggested that errors are inevitable in a job where decisions must often be made with incomplete information and grave consequences. Bush emphasized the importance of principle, alliances and restraint, while Clinton focused on the need to learn from failures and recognize the human cost of inaction.

Their reflections underscored the enduring weight of presidential decisions in foreign affairs — from choosing war or restraint, to pursuing peace, to confronting humanitarian catastrophe. Decades after leaving office, both men portrayed the presidency as a role defined not only by victories and policy achievements, but also by unresolved conflicts and painful regrets.

*By [Reporter Name]*

Former President George H.W. Bush has raised a striking question about one of the defining decisions of his presidency, saying he wonders whether Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein should have been forced to surrender at the end of the 1991 Gulf War rather than being allowed to remain in power after U.S.-led forces drove Iraq from Kuwait.

Bush’s reflection adds a notable coda to a conflict long viewed by many of his advisers as a model of limited-war strategy: a broad international coalition, a clear objective, and a swift military victory. But the decision not to march on Baghdad—and not to compel Saddam’s removal—remained one of the most debated judgments of Bush’s presidency, particularly after the United States returned to war with Iraq under his son, President George W. Bush, in 2003.

In remarks that revisit that moment, Bush said he had wondered whether Saddam should have been made to formally surrender after Iraqi forces were routed in Kuwait. The comment stops short of saying the United States should have occupied Iraq or toppled Saddam outright, but it underscores the lingering uncertainty around a choice that shaped Middle East politics for more than a decade.

At the same time, former President Bill Clinton has offered his own reflection on an unresolved foreign-policy ambition, expressing regret over the failure to secure a lasting Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement during his presidency. Clinton invested heavily in the peace process, culminating in the 2000 Camp David summit and subsequent negotiations, but the talks ended without a final accord.

Together, the comments from the two former presidents highlight the long afterlife of major foreign-policy decisions—and non-decisions—whose consequences continued to reverberate well beyond their years in office.

Bush, who assembled a multinational coalition after Saddam’s invasion of Kuwait in August 1990, ordered Operation Desert Storm in January 1991 after Iraq ignored international demands to withdraw. The war ended quickly, with Iraqi forces expelled from Kuwait in a matter of weeks. Bush’s administration chose not to continue the campaign to Baghdad, arguing that doing so would have exceeded the United Nations mandate, fractured the coalition and risked a costly occupation.

At the time, Bush and his national security team defended the decision as prudent and disciplined. They feared that removing Saddam could destabilize Iraq, empower Iran, and pull U.S. forces into an open-ended effort to govern a divided country. Those concerns later became central to debates over the 2003 invasion, when the younger Bush administration toppled Saddam but struggled with the insurgency and sectarian conflict that followed.

Still, the 1991 decision carried consequences of its own. Saddam survived the war, brutally suppressed uprisings by Shiites in southern Iraq and Kurds in the north, and remained under a web of sanctions, weapons inspections and no-fly zones through the 1990s. Critics argued that leaving him in power guaranteed future crises. Defenders countered that the alternative—an American occupation of Iraq without a clear plan or broad international authorization—could have been even more dangerous.

Bush’s new remark suggests that even the architect of the 1991 war’s limited aims saw reason, in hindsight, to question whether Saddam should have faced a more explicit capitulation.

Clinton’s comments, meanwhile, revisit another defining diplomatic struggle of the post-Cold War era. His administration helped broker the Oslo-era negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians and hosted Israeli and Palestinian leaders in repeated attempts to reach a final-status agreement. The most high-profile effort came in July 2000, when Clinton brought Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to Camp David.

The summit failed to resolve the core issues dividing the two sides, including borders, Jerusalem, Palestinian refugees and security arrangements. Subsequent talks narrowed some gaps but did not produce an agreement before Clinton left office in January 2001. Soon after, the Second Intifada intensified, reshaping Israeli and Palestinian politics and leaving the peace process deeply weakened.

Clinton has often described the failure to reach a deal as one of the greatest disappointments of his presidency. His latest reflection reinforces how close he believed the parties came—and how costly he viewed the collapse of negotiations. Supporters of the Clinton effort have argued that the framework discussed in 2000 and early 2001 foreshadowed many later proposals for a two-state solution. Critics, however, have long debated whether the proposals were politically viable, whether the parties were prepared to make historic compromises, and whether the United States misread the pressures facing both sides.

The reflections by Bush and Clinton come at a time when U.S. foreign policy from the 1990s is receiving renewed scrutiny. The Gulf War, the containment of Iraq, the Oslo peace process and the limits of American power in the Middle East all remain central to understanding subsequent decades of conflict.

For Bush, the question is whether a war widely considered successful ended too soon—or ended without sufficient guarantees about Saddam’s future behavior. For Clinton, the question is whether one of the most ambitious diplomatic efforts of his presidency fell short because of timing, leadership, mistrust or the sheer difficulty of reconciling competing national claims.

Neither former president’s regret is simple. Bush’s hesitation reflects the tension between military victory and political endgame, while Clinton’s regret reflects the frustration of diplomacy in a conflict where even intense presidential involvement could not produce a final settlement.

Both remarks underscore a shared reality of presidential decision-making: the most consequential choices are often made amid uncertainty, and their full weight is measured only years later.
